While wage increases might be a trigger for a shift for some companies, the real factor here is the evolution of money and the market penetration of the debit card.

Fast food started on the fast-track to automation in the era of the much-loved Automat, way back at the start of the 20th century. Started by the famous Horn & Hardart, automats provided a simple, convenient, front-end automation for food service through the standardization of the production of food and the use of racks of refrigerated or heated glass door cabinets with coin-operated locks. By producing standard food in batches, it also allowed for more back-end efficiency allowing for competitive prices while still retaining the appeal of the sit-down restaurant with use of actual china and silverware. Though limited to cities, the model proved popular across a broad demographic and quickly spread across the world. Rich, middle-class, and poor all loved the automat and it was celebrated in art, film, and even cartoons.

But after WWII food prices increased while governments refused to introduce higher denominations in coins, favoring expanded paper money use. This created a problem for coin operated vending technology generally, limiting the range of products that could use that distribution as a reliable method of handling paper bills would not emerge until the late 1970s. Automat use became unwieldy as more and more coins were needed and eventually some restaurants switched to the use of tokens, which meant a human service person to exchange bills, severely detracting from the original convenience. Automats went into decline in favor of a counter-service model and the return of a set of employees once considered obsolete simply because of the need to handle paper money.

The 'counter service' model of the American burger restaurant evolved from the sit-down counter diner model and originated with the White Mana restaurant that first appeared in the 1939 New York World's Fair --billed as the first 'scientifically managed' eatery and the 'diner of the future'. (it later produced two competing restaurants in NJ that remain in a well known feud to this day, the White Mana based on the original building and the White Manna that claims the original food recipes and techniques) Trading the sit-down counter for order and pick-up counters, this facilitated faster throughput and enabled the use of a drive-through model. As the automat went into decline, this model took off with the growth of suburbs and increasing automobile ownership, becoming the standard for fast-food today. But the compulsion to streamline their food production and customer processing always had fast food restaurants experimenting with new methods and more automation.

By the '60s the Japanese had developed novel methods of front-end order processing using conventional vending machines as push-button menus that would output item tickets. You would compose your order with those tickets and just drop them off at an order counter then wait for your order number to be called. You could even buy them in advance or trade them with other people. They were given out as marketing incentives and people would often give the homeless these food tickets instead of change. This greatly reduced the number of necessary front-end workers and the size of counter space needed and the method is still in use today. (there's a sort of nostalgia for electromechanical vending machines in Japan) But it never made it to the US or Europe, again possibly because of the continued resistance to higher denomination coinage.

In the late '70s many large fast-food chains began experimenting with computer-assisted ordering using various order terminal designs but, even with the advent of paper money scanners, they were too cumbersome for the average customer. The real breakthrough was the introduction of high resolution graphic touch screens and the replacement of physical currency altogether by the introduction of debit cards. But, again, the use of the technology was held-up, partly by the cost of hardware (thanks to the US computer industry basically selling-off all its flat panel display tech to Japan then Reagan era trade wars with Japan keeping flat screens expensive) but primarily by banks. Debit card use was long limited to the higher-end of society because banks treated it as a premium service. By the '80s the predominant consumer demographic for fast-food had become the lower middle-class and poor with a slowly growing segment of elderly. It wasn't until the '90s that banks, pressured by the backlash they had created by neglecting even basic banking services in low-income neighborhoods, finally started expanding debit card use generally. Only by the start of the 21st century had debit card use penetrated the fast-food demographic to where, finally, automated front-end solutions started looking viable.

So the shift was inevitably going to happen. The technology had been at-hand since the '80s. It was just waiting for enough of the poor and the elderly to start using debit cards. It was only a matter of when, not if. Maybe the politics was a trigger, but it was going to happen this decade anyway.

Indeed, we are five years away from replacing even the debit card and the pick-up counter. Emerging right now is 'smartlock' technology and digital currency exchange that, together, bring us right back to the automat. Right now you can build a restaurant where all you have is a set of cabinets opened using your smartphone as a digital key. You can buy what's ready-made or you can use your smartphone to custom order food and collect it at a pick-up 'smartlocker' displaying your order name/number. This is already being demonstrated by a start-up restaurant chain called Eatsa started in San Francisco and now in New York and Washington DC. I think this will not only be significant for traditional fast-food but also for the hole-in-the-wall ethnic food restaurants common in the city. It will radically reduce the costs of creating a restaurant because it radically minimizes your storefront needs as well as employee overhead. All you now need to create a fast food restaurant is a cooking space and a wall space for some touch screens and pick-up lockers. I anticipate that this will also integrate into self-driving automobiles. Your car will become the front-end for fast-food restaurants, allowing you to order and pay while on the move. Restaurants will push ads and offers as your car comes into their proximity. The drive through pick-up will have nothing but an automatic cabinet that recognizes your car as your drive up and pushes your order to the door.
I only wish this had happened sooner.
